newsitem.title: UK: Dlr stuck in Europe as jobs distract from euro row.
newsitem.headline: Dlr stuck in Europe as jobs distract from euro row.

text.p: The dollar was mired in tiny ranges against the mark in Europe on Thursday as traders shunned extreme currency positions ahead of Friday's release of key monthly employment reports from the U.S. and Germany.

The fresh uncertainties shrouding the shape, size and timing of the single European currency lost centre stage to these pivotal economic reports. But a lack of consensus about their likely impact confined prices to established bands.
"The political row in Europe is in many respects ambiguous for the mark and the impact of German economic data is finely balanced," said Paul Meggyesi at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Meggyesi, who is a senior currency strategist at DMG, said seasonal considerations had some in the market leaning toward weaker-than-consensus U.S. payrolls totals for May, but this in itself increased the risk of positive dollar reaction if the data comes in as expected.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect a 219,000 rise in non-farm payrolls during the month. The Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee meets July 1 and 2 amid talk of an interest rate rise.
Leaks from two German papers of an unadjusted 90,000 drop in unemployed in May were confirmed today by Labour office sources. The papers said this translates to a 60,000 rise in adjusted jobless.

At 1510 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7297/02 marks compared with 1.7308/13 late Wednesday and confined to a range of less than half a pfennig just under 1.73 marks for the bulk of the European session. It was softer against a more robust Japanese yen at 115.60/70 compared with 116.22/32 yesterday.

Traders said hawkish comments from Federal Reserve president Alfred Broaddus late Wednesday kept the prospect of another imminent Fed rate rise alive. Broaddus said the economic risks were still to the upside, he said he wasn't sure if rates were high enough to keep a lid on growth and the higher dollar alone could not be relied upon to slow the economy.
"I think another U.S. rate rise is still in the pipeline before the Fed backs off and monitors its impact through the Summer," said one trader at a Dutch firm here.

In Germany, the impact of jobless and other German economic data remains confusing because of the complication of monetary union. Strong data may increase pressure for higher interest rates but it improves the chances of Germany meeting EMU budget goals and hence the replacement of the mark by the euro in 1999.
News today showed first-quarter German gross domestic product slowed to 1.4 percent year-on-year from 1.9 percent in Q4 but this was distorted lower by three fewer workdays in 1997.
"The political story in Europe is also ambiguous to a degree, even though the rule of thumb for now is that it will lead to a punctual but softer euro," said Meggyesi at Deutsche.
"If Germany is pushed too hard on issues like abandoning the stability pact, this could well lead to an EMU delay and you would not want to be too short of marks in that case."
The dollar has risen more than three pfennigs this week as Germany budgetary problems and a new Socialist government in France have raised speculation of a broad-based start to EMU.
Elsewhere, the yen made independent gains on the latest Japanese trade data and jitters about a rate rise there.

Japan recorded a trade surplus of 41.16 billion yen for the first 20 days of May, compared with a deficit of 180.94 billion in the same period last year. Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita said, meantime, the central bank was prepared to act pre-emptively on interest rates.
The yen's gains were broad-based and the mark/yen cross rate fell to a two-week low at 66.85.
Sterling/mark was underpinned as traders awaited the outcome tomorrow of the Bank of England's new policy-making council amid some expectations of another quarter-point interest rate rise.
